q: Atoms of elements are rarely found by themselves in nature.
e: Everything around us is made up of elements, molecules, or compounds, as elements interact to form new substances.

q: The attractive forces that hold atoms together in compounds are also known as intermolecular forces.
e: The attractive forces that hold atoms together in compounds are known as chemical bonds.

q: The outermost shell electrons of atoms are the basis for understanding the joining of atoms.
e: These valence electrons interact to form the forces of attraction that hold atoms together.

q: According to the Aufbau principle, electrons are filled in the higher energy atomic orbitals before filling lower energy ones.
e: The Aufbau principle states that electrons are filled in the lower energy atomic orbitals before filling higher energy ones.

q: The order of filling the orbitals is given as 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p.
e: This sequence follows the Aufbau principle for building up the electronic configuration of atoms.

q: Pauli's exclusion principle states that no more than three electrons can occupy the same orbital.
e: Pauli's exclusion principle states that no more than two electrons can occupy the same orbital.

q: Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins.
e: This is a requirement of Pauli's exclusion principle for electrons sharing the same orbital space.

q: Hund's rule states that every orbital in a subshell is doubly occupied before any one orbital is singly occupied.
e: Hund's rule states that every orbital in a subshell is singly occupied with one electron before any one orbital is doubly occupied.

q: The s subshell has only one spherical-shaped orbital.
e: This single orbital can hold a maximum of two electrons.

q: There are five dumbbell-shaped p orbitals in an atom.
e: There are three dumbbell-shaped p orbitals ($p_x$, $p_y$, $p_z$), while d orbitals have double dumbbell-shapes.

q: Each p subshell can be filled with a maximum of 10 electrons.
e: Each p subshell can be filled with 6 electrons, whereas the d subshell holds 10 electrons.

q: For an atom, the number of valence electrons is equal to its group number in the Periodic Table.
e: For example, carbon is in Group IV and has 4 valence electrons.

q: Whenever a chemical bond forms, atoms lose, gain, or share electrons in order to achieve the stable electronic structures of noble gases.
e: This tendency to achieve eight electrons in the valence shell is known as the octet rule.

q: The octet rule strictly applies to all d-block elements without exceptions.
e: The octet rule does not apply to d-block elements.

q: Electronegativity is a measure of the ability of an atom to attract the shared electrons to itself.
e: The greater an element's electronegativity, the stronger its attractive power to electrons will be.

q: Electron affinity is the amount of energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom.
e: Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom; ionisation energy is the energy required to remove an electron.

q: Elements having high electron affinity easily gain electrons, resulting in the formation of anions.
e: Conversely, elements with low ionisation energy easily lose electrons to form cations.

q: Generally, the higher the first ionisation energy of an element, the lower is its electronegativity.
e: Generally, the higher the first ionisation energy of an element, the greater is its electronegativity.

q: The three main types of chemical bonding are ionic bonding, covalent bonding, and hydrogen bonding.
e: The three main types of chemical bonding are ionic bonding, covalent bonding, and metallic bonding.

q: In general, an ionic bond is stronger than a covalent bond.
e: Ionic bonds involve strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions in a lattice.

q: The hydrogen bond is the strongest intermolecular force followed by van der Waals forces.
e: While weaker than covalent or ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds are the strongest among intermolecular forces.

q: Among van der Waals forces, dipole-dipole interactions are the weakest intermolecular forces that can be found in all substances.
e: London dispersion forces are the weakest intermolecular forces that can be found in all substances.

q: Most bonds are 100% ionic or 100% covalent.
e: Most bonds have at least some degree of both ionic and covalent character.

q: In atoms, there are K, L, M, N main shells and each main shell can be divided into s, p, d, and f subshells.
e: These subshells contain spaces for electrons called orbitals.

q: Only core electrons can take part in chemical bonding.
e: Only valence electrons can take part in chemical bonding.
